title: Carried by memory
hookLine: for a long time, tradition says, the teaching was memorized and chanted by reciters, not written
carry: the binding of an unwritten book
last: HELD BY MANY MOUTHS, NOT JUST ONE MEMORY.

cards: "Thus have I heard." Open the Long Discourses at the beginning and that is how the first sutta starts, and the same words open sutta after sutta.
Tradition says the voice is Ananda's, at the council, reciting what he heard the Buddha say. It's a strange way to start a holy text. Not: thus it is.
Not: thus it was written. Thus I heard it. The teaching opens by telling you how it reached you: through someone's ears, and someone's memory.
Today, how the teaching traveled before it was written down.

teach.h: A TEXT WAS A GROUP OF PEOPLE.
teach.b: Tradition says that after the council, groups of monks took on different collections of the teaching and learned them by heart, chanting them together and teaching them to their students, who taught their own.
A text was not a book on a shelf. It was a group of people who could say it.

Read the suttas and you notice the repetition: the same passage again and again, lists of three things, four things, eight things, whole paragraphs repeated with one word changed. On paper, that can feel slow.
Out loud, it helps a memory hold its shape. Repetition works like the binding of an unwritten book.
The Vinaya tells of an elder named Purana who arrived after the council was over. The elders invited him to accept what they had recited.

He said it was well recited, but he would remember the teaching the way he himself had heard it from the Buddha. The text records his answer and moves on. Even in the first generation, memory came in more than one voice.
At last, the chronicles of Sri Lanka say, in a time of hardship, monks there wrote the texts down so they would not be lost.
Until then, tradition says, they had been carried in people.
Heard that way, the long stretch before writing looks less like a gap than a kind of care: the teaching was kept alive by being said aloud, by people who had given their lives to it.

how: In Theravada monasteries, monks and novices learn suttas and verses by heart and chant them together, and some monks learn whole collections.

games.q: you're Purana, arriving after the council is over. the elders invite you to accept what they recited. what do you say?
o: say it was well recited, but you'll keep the teaching as you heard it.
ask them to hold the council again.
games.why: he praises the recitation and still keeps his own memory of the Buddha's words. the Vinaya records it without comment.

practice: Take today's line, thus have I heard, or a short line of your own from a teaching or a poem you love, and say it aloud three times. Then close your eyes and say it once more without looking; if a word slips, look, and try again.

wordCard.voice: Reciters. They carried the teaching by memory, chanting it together and passing it on by mouth before it was written. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: thus have I heard. the opening of the suttas, said in Ananda's voice.

carryVoice: Your line: the binding of an unwritten book. The words lived in people before they lived on a page. See you tomorrow.
